paragraphs.text: Chew et al. (2013) used the term 'TUBB3 E410K syndrome' for the disorder caused by the E410K substitution in TUBB3. Its features are congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles, facial weakness, developmental delay and intellectual disability, and a progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Affected individuals may also have Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia) and stereotyped midface hypoplasia. Some also have vocal cord paralysis, tracheomalacia, and cyclic vomiting.

paragraphs.text: Tischfield et al. (2010) studied 6 pedigrees with the TUBB3 E410K substitution. All patients had severe CFEOM3 and congenital facial weakness. They also had more severe dysgenesis of the corpus callosum than patients with other TUBB3 mutations, together with mild to moderate intellectual, social, and behavioral impairment. In the second to third decade, the oldest E410K patient developed weakness and sensory loss in the lower extremities. He had no congenital contractures. Tischfield et al. (2010) also reviewed brain MRI from patients with TUBB3 mutations. Common findings were dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, anterior commissure, and internal capsule, generalized loss of white matter, and dysmorphic basal ganglia. No patient had cortical dysplasia or evidence of a cortical migration defect. In general, the more severe the corpus callosum dysgenesis, the more severe the intellectual and behavioral impairment.

paragraphs.text: Chew et al. (2013) described the phenotypes of 8 unrelated individuals with the TUBB3 E410K substitution in detail. All had congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles, facial weakness, developmental delay and intellectual disability, and a progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy confirmed by electrophysiology. The authors added Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia) and stereotyped midface hypoplasia to the phenotype. Some patients also had vocal cord paralysis, tracheomalacia, and cyclic vomiting. On neuroimaging, the corpus callosum and anterior commissure were thin. The olfactory sulci, olfactory bulbs, and oculomotor and facial nerves were hypoplastic or absent. The authors considered these findings consistent with underlying defects in axon guidance and maintenance.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2018) reported a 31-year-old Japanese woman who had been diagnosed with atypical Moebius syndrome. The diagnosis was based on congenital facial weakness and external ophthalmoplegia that spared abduction. At age 23 years she had a femoral neck fracture, and investigation showed osteoporosis caused by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. She also had borderline intellectual disability, cyclic vomiting, and syncope with cough, and her sense of smell had been reduced since childhood. Brain MRI showed abnormal morphology of the corpus callosum and pons, and both oculomotor nerves and both facial nerves were hypoplastic.

paragraphs.text: Grant et al. (2019) studied 7 unrelated individuals with the TUBB3 E410K syndrome: 4 children and 3 adults. All had intellectual and social disabilities, and none had a cortical malformation. On structural and diffusion MRI, the patients had smaller corpus callosum volume and lower network efficiency than 22 controls. In every patient, the corticospinal tract followed an aberrant course, and the long segment of the dorsal language network was absent on both sides.

paragraphs.text: Jia et al. (2022) described 2 unrelated Chinese Han probands with CFEOM, neither with a family history of the disorder: an 11-year-old boy and a 19-year-old woman. Both had bilateral ptosis, exotropia, limited horizontal and vertical eye movements, corneal exposure, facial weakness, intellectual impairment, and impaired gait. On MRI, both had absent or dysplastic olfactory bulbs and sulci, hypoplasia of the oculomotor nerve and extraocular muscles, and absent facial nerves. Both also had malformations of the corpus callosum, anterior commissure, and lateral ventricles. The boy had cryptorchidism, and infertility was found in the woman at follow-up. Both probands met diagnostic criteria for Kallmann syndrome, as did a third patient carrying a TUBB3 R262H variant.

paragraphs.text: Tischfield et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous 1228G-A transition in the TUBB3 gene, resulting in a glu410-to-lys (E410K) substitution, in 6 pedigrees with CFEOM3 and additional neurologic features. In each case the mutation arose de novo, presenting as sporadic disease or through presumed germline mosaicism. All patients had severe CFEOM3, congenital facial weakness, and dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, with mild to moderate intellectual, social, and behavioral impairment. In reticulocyte lysate, the E410K mutant formed heterodimers that cycled like wildtype. In yeast, the substitution altered microtubule dynamics and reduced accumulation of the kinesins Kip3p and Kip2p at microtubule plus ends.
